result.abstractText:
Background

Management of a degenerative meniscal tear (DMT) or symptoms consistent with early knee osteoarthritis (OA) frequently deviates from international clinical practice guidelines, which recommend education and exercise as first-line treatments and strongly advise against arthroscopic partial meniscectomy. There is a need for implementation strategies to support the uptake of evidence-based care.

Methods

A systematic, four-step intervention development process was used to guide development of a multi-faceted implementation intervention targeting both individuals with a DMT or early knee OA and their general practitioners (GPs). The process integrated behavioural theory, stakeholder perspectives and evidence on intervention effectiveness. Target behaviours were identified through a literature review and stakeholder consultation. Previously conducted qualitative interviews with 17 GPs and 11 people with DMT were re-analysed and mapped to the Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF) to identify behavioural barriers and enablers to the targeted behaviours. Behaviour change techniques (BCTs) and intervention components were then selected to address these determinants. Stakeholder input was incorporated to enhance acceptability and feasibility.

Results

The resulting intervention aims to promote guideline-concordant management of a DMT and early knee OA. A programme theory to guide implementation was developed to describe hypothesised mechanisms of action, and candidate outcome measures were identified to support future evaluation and assess the mediating mechanisms of behaviour change.

Conclusion

Using a systematic, theory-informed and stakeholder-engaged approach, we developed a multi-faceted intervention to support delivery and uptake of evidence-based care for DMT and early knee OA. The intervention comprised GP educational workshops and resources to support an 'enhanced consultation', alongside referral to an early 'best practice' physiotherapy session. Patients received both components. The intervention was designed to be feasible, acceptable and locally relevant, but requires further testing to assess implementation and potential for scale-up in clinical practice.

Lived experience or public contribution

Stakeholder contributions played a central role in this study. People with lived experience of degenerative meniscal tears and/or knee OA (n = 6) and healthcare professional stakeholders (n = 15) were consulted during group discussions and individual meetings. Stakeholders informed every step of the development process, aiming to ensure the final intervention was feasible, acceptable and adapted to the local context.

result.abstractText:
Purpose

To develop and externally validate a peri-ablational contrast-enhanced CT radiomics model for predicting early hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression after microwave ablation (MWA) and to assess its incremental value over clinical predictors.

Methods

This retrospective multicenter study included 376 patients in training (n = 235), internal validation (n = 60), and external validation (n = 81) cohorts. Early progression was defined as local tumor progression or new intrahepatic HCC within 1 year after MWA. Radiomics features were extracted from 5-mm peri-ablational regions on multiphasic CT obtained 1-2 months after MWA. Six machine-learning algorithms and phase combinations were evaluated. The selected radiomics model was combined with independent clinical predictors. Discrimination, calibration, clinical utility, and model interpretability were assessed.

Results

The arterial-plus-portal venous phase (AP + PP) multilayer perceptron model achieved AUCs of 0.857, 0.815, and 0.903 in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively, with performance comparable to the three-phase model. Log10 AFP and tumor size > 2 cm were independent clinical predictors. The combined clinical-radiomics model achieved AUCs of 0.926, 0.884, and 0.963, respectively. In external validation, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were 84.2%, 96.8%, and 93.8%, respectively. SHAP analysis identified the radiomics score as the most influential predictor.

Conclusion

Peri-ablational AP + PP CT radiomics combined with AFP and tumor size demonstrated good discrimination for early HCC progression after MWA and may facilitate individualized risk assessment, pending further validation.

result.abstractText: Purpose To evaluate the performance of Sybil, a Medical Open Network for Artificial Intelligence (MONAI)-based nodule model, and their combination for 1-year lung cancer detection in two screening cohorts: the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) and the Pamplona International Early Lung Cancer Action Program (P-IELCAP). Materials and Methods Baseline low-dose CT (LDCT) examinations from the NLST and the P-IELCAP were analyzed. A prespecified OR-stacked composite model combining Sybil, a MONAI-based nodule model, and a safety-net rule (MONAI-detected nodule > 6 mm with detection confidence > 0.95) was developed and evaluated for 1-year lung cancer detection. Model discrimination was assessed by using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and operating-point performance metrics were calculated. Results A total of 5110 baseline LDCT examinations were analyzed, including 2343 from NLST and 2767 from P-IELCAP, with 65 lung cancers diagnosed within 1 year. Mean age, mean pack-years, and percentage of female participants were 61.6 years ± 5.1 (SD), 57.3 pack-years ± 24.8, and 39.4% (923 of 2343), respectively, in NLST and 56.0 years ± 9.5, 34.4 pack-years ± 21.5, and 28.6% (791 of 2767), respectively, in P-IELCAP. Lung cancer incidence (per 1000 person-years) was higher in NLST than in P-IELCAP (17.7 vs 8.7; P = .006). Mean Sybil 1-year lung cancer probabilities (scaled by 1000 for presentation) were also higher in NLST than in P-IELCAP (16.4 vs 9.9; P < .01). Sybil achieved an AUC of 0.93 in both cohorts, whereas the MONAI-based model achieved AUCs of 0.90 in NLST and 0.79 in P-IELCAP. The composite model missed two of 65 1-year lung cancers while correctly classifying 2731 of 4965 (55.0%) noncancer examinations as negative, yielding a sensitivity of 63 of 65 (96.9%) and a positive predictive value of 63 of 2297 (2.7%). Conclusion For 1-year lung cancer detection with LDCT, the composite AI model achieved high sensitivity while maintaining acceptable specificity. result.abstractText:
Background

Targeted lung cancer screening programmes in the United Kingdom use multivariable risk models to identify high-risk individuals. However, public acceptability of targeting screening by risk using eligibility criteria, such as age and smoking history, remains unclear, including the psychological and behavioural consequences of eligibility disclosure.

Aim

To explore UK public attitudes toward the acceptability of current risk-based eligibility criteria for lung cancer screening and the anticipated psychological and behavioural responses to eligibility disclosure.

Methods

A qualitative study was conducted as the second phase of a sequential explanatory design. Semi-structured telephone interviews were held with 28 UK adults aged 45-77 years between January-April 2024. Participants were purposively sampled for diversity in demographics, smoking history, and prior acceptability questionnaire responses. Interviews were analysed using applied thematic analysis informed by the Theoretical Framework of Acceptability.

Results

Criteria were generally acceptable when perceived as evidence-based and logical, particularly age and smoking history. However, participants expected flexibility, suggested expanding inclusion criteria and had concerns about fairness and discrimination especially regarding ethnicity and education. Eligibility was anticipated to motivate screening attendance but also cause worry; the prospect of ineligibility often led to feelings of exclusion, anxiety, and disappointment. Participants emphasised the need for clear, evidence-based communication of the rationale and individual risk, alongside alternative options or support for those who are ineligible.

Conclusions

Clear and transparent communication of the rationales underpinning eligibility criteria, provided by the screening programme and trusted health professionals, are essential for improving public acceptability and individual understanding of eligibility status. These strategies should also mitigate against potential stigma, perceived discrimination, and over-reassurance, while ensuring appropriate safety-netting and risk management for those who are ineligible. Tailored messaging and pathways may optimise engagement, trust, and psychological wellbeing within lung cancer screening programmes.

Patient or public contribution

The research team sought the views of eight public and patient representatives with lung cancer experience (either personally or being a carer) during study conception. They endorsed the research objectives, helped to develop participant-facing interview questions and gave feedback on the appropriateness of the design, agreeing that in-depth interviews would best capture perceptions of the acceptability of risk-based eligibility criteria.

result.title: Segmentation-perturbation propagation in pretrained foundation-model embeddings versus IBSI-aligned radiomics for radiologist-assessed lung-nodule malignancy classification on the LIDC-IDRI cohort.
result.authorString: Wanni Arachchige ICK.

authorAffiliation.affiliation: Independent Researcher, Adelaide, , South Australia, Australia.

result.abstractText:
Objective

Pretrained foundation-model (FM) embeddings are proposed as robust alternatives to handcrafted radiomic features, yet whether they better withstand segmentation-mask variability, the perturbation that radiomics intraclass-correlation (ICC) filtering exists to address, has not been tested head-to-head. We quantified how segmentation-mask perturbation propagates into feature reproducibility and downstream malignancy discrimination for FM embeddings and Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI)-compliant radiomics measured on a common cohort. Approach. Two 2D FM encoders (BiomedCLIP; RadImageNet ResNet50) were compared against IBSI-compliant radiomics (3D, 107 features; 2D, 102 features) on the full eligible Lung Image Database Consortium and Image Database Resource Initiative (LIDC-IDRI) cohort: 556 lung nodules (300 malignant, 256 benign from radiologist consensus ratings, not pathology) from 399 patients. Up to thirteen perturbed masks per nodule (up to four reader masks, eight synthetic, one Dice-calibrated) were generated, and ICC(2,1) was computed across the ten perturbation conditions available for every nodule. Malignancy classification used L2-regularized logistic regression with patient-grouped five-fold cross-validation and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on every area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Main results. Radiomics outperformed both foundation models on discrimination (AUC 0.940 and 0.930 for radiomics-2D/3D versus 0.833 BiomedCLIP and 0.798 RadImageNet; all radiomics-versus-FM differences significant by DeLong test, p≤10^(-7)). On perturbation stability the foundation models diverged: BiomedCLIP was statistically indistinguishable from radiomics (93.8% versus 90.2-92.5% stable features) and the most stable paradigm, whereas RadImageNet was significantly less stable (75.0%). A pre-specified diameter-stratified analysis showed the radiomics advantage narrows, and partly reverses, within size-matched strata; decision-curve analysis favoured radiomics. Significance. Two-dimensional foundation-model embeddings offered no discrimination advantage over IBSI radiomics under segmentation perturbation, and greater stability did not translate into greater accuracy. Perturbation stability is therefore decoupled from task-informativeness, and comparative benchmarks should report patient-grouped, size-stratified, calibration-aware metrics, not aggregate accuracy alone. .

result.abstractText:
Background

Socially assistive robots are increasingly explored in health care, but evidence from routine pediatric outpatient settings remains limited.

Objective

This study examined how contextual support and human facilitation shaped visitor interaction with the Temi V3 robot and which sociotechnical conditions were associated with practical acceptance according to staff.

Methods

A mixed methods pilot combined structured behavioral observation across baseline, poster support, and staff facilitation conditions with 4 staff focus group interviews. The observation unit was a visitor passage through the lobby zone; the qualitative sample comprised 12 staff members with direct exposure to the robot. Quantitative indicators were analyzed descriptively, and staff interviews underwent deductive-inductive qualitative content analysis.

Results

In total, 675 visitor passages (children: n=398, 59% and adults: n=277, 41%) were recorded (baseline: n=257; poster support: n=160; and staff facilitation: n=258). Looking at the robot increased from 8 (3.1%) passages at baseline to 30 (18.8%) with poster support and 80 (31%) with staff facilitation. Screen or app use increased from 2 (0.8%) passages at baseline to 4 (2.5%) with poster support and 14 (5.4%) with staff facilitation. Observer notes indicated stronger visible responsiveness among children, although age category was not linked to individual behavior codes. Staff emphasized role clarity, child and family value, human mediation, functional reliability, multilingual content, and organizational ownership.

Conclusions

Observed visitor interaction was higher with poster support and staff facilitation than at baseline. These descriptive findings and staff perceptions informed a provisional 4-domain framework comprising role clarity, interaction affordance, social mediation, and organizational embedding. The framework identifies potential implementation priorities; visitors' own experiences and acceptance require direct assessment.

result.abstractText:
Purpose

Accurate quantification of inflammatory cells in Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS)-stained kidney transplant biopsies is essential for Banff classification but remains subjective and labor-intensive. To address this, the MONKEY challenge benchmarked deep learning (DL) methods for automated detection of mononuclear leukocytes and their subtypes.

Materials and methods

A multicenter dataset of 118 biopsies with co-registered PAS and immunohistochemically restained slides, comprising over 131,000 annotated cells, was used. The algorithms were evaluated on hold-out validation and test set using Free-response Receiver Operating Characteristic (FROC) analysis, alongside precision, recall, and F1-scores.

Results

Across diverse architectures, performance converged, with the top models achieving F1-scores up to 0.75 for overall detection. Lymphocyte detection performed well (F1 up to 0.78), whereas monocyte detection remained more challenging (F1 up to 0.47). To explore the potential clinical applicability of automated inflammatory cell detection, the winning model was integrated with renal tissue segmentation models, enabling compartment-specific evaluation and quantitative assessment of Banff-related lesions. In an independent multicenter cohort of 180 kidney transplant biopsies, DL-derived quantitative measurements demonstrated strong correlations with consensus pathologist scoring for several inflammation-related Banff lesions, particularly total inflammation and interstitial inflammation.

Conclusions

This study establishes the first multicenter, PAS-based, IHC-validated benchmark for inflammatory cell detection and provides a clinically grounded resource to support the development of robust, generalizable AI systems for transplant pathology. Beyond benchmark performance, our extended tissue-specific analyses demonstrate that inflammatory cell detection on routine PAS slides can be anatomically contextualized and translated into quantitative measurements that align with conventional Banff lesion assessment, providing a foundation for future AI-assisted evaluation of kidney transplant biopsies.

result.abstractText: Falls among older adults represent a major public health concern with substantial clinical, societal, and economic implications. People living with dementia (PlwD) are disproportionately affected, reflecting the combined impact of cognitive, motor, and pharmacological vulnerabilities. Traditional fall risk assessment tools have demonstrated limitations in capturing the complex, dynamic risk profiles of people living with dementia, highlighting the need for technological innovation in prediction, detection, and prevention. Despite advances in gerontechnology, evidence specific to dementia remains limited. To address this gap, a scoping review was conducted following PRISMA-ScR and Joanna Briggs Institute guidelines. Comprehensive searches across Scopus, Medline, Embase, APA PsycINFO, and CINAHL identified thirteen peer-reviewed studies (2015-2025) evaluating technology-based approaches for fall prediction, detection, or prevention among people living with dementia or populations used to model dementia-related functional impairments. Data were extracted and synthesized thematically by technological function. Thirteen studies met inclusion criteria, encompassing pressure-sensitive platforms, technology-enabled preventive interventions, wearable inertial measurement units, and ambient radar/vision-based systems, with the latter two most common. Sample sizes ranged from 3-309 participants with varying dementia severity. Wearables demonstrated strong fall detection performance in controlled laboratory settings but were limited by adherence challenges and reduced ecological validity. Ambient and radar-based systems demonstrated feasibility yet raised privacy and scalability concerns. Pressure-sensitive platforms showed promise for identifying pre-fall risk states but lacked clinical validation. result.abstractText: Primary thyroid lymphoma (PTL) is a rare thyroid malignancy that may present with respiratory symptoms overlapping with cardiopulmonary disease, contributing to delayed diagnosis. We report a 78-year-old woman with chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart failure, and prior lung cancer whose worsening dyspnea was repeatedly attributed to underlying cardiopulmonary conditions. She subsequently developed dysphonia and dysphagia with a rapidly enlarging thyroid mass requiring tracheostomy for airway protection. Prior computed tomography imaging obtained during multiple evaluations for cardiopulmonary symptoms incidentally demonstrated subtle thyroid enlargement with progressive interval growth on retrospective review. Core biopsy confirmed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and staging established stage IIIE disease. Given her age and comorbidities, a dose-reduced regimen of rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone was initiated. Despite treatment, her condition deteriorated rapidly, and she died shortly thereafter. This case underscores how overlapping comorbidities can obscure PTL presentation until advanced airway compromise develops. In patients with persistent respiratory symptoms despite appropriate cardiopulmonary management, careful review of prior imaging is critical because subtle thyroid enlargement may otherwise be overlooked.

result.abstractText: Precision oncology is redefining cancer therapeutics worldwide. In Australia, the integration of genomic medicine into routine clinical oncology remains inconsistently constrained by fragmented funding mechanisms, regional disparities, and a limited workforce. Understanding these structural and policy challenges is crucial for transitioning toward a sustainable, equitable genomic health ecosystem. This narrative review synthesizes evidence from national policy frameworks, peer-reviewed literature, and translational oncology initiatives to examine the current state of precision oncology in Australia. Key domains of analysis include clinical practice patterns, access and equity, infrastructure, data governance, regulatory oversight, and health-policy reform. Although major initiatives, such as Omico's Precision Oncology Screening Platform Enabling Clinical Trials (PrOSPeCT) platform, the ZERO Childhood Cancer Program, and the forthcoming national coordination body Genomics Australia, demonstrate substantial progress, significant implementation barriers persist. Australia stands on the cusp of realizing a genomics-enabled model of cancer care. Consolidation of national governance under Genomics Australia, expansion of Medicare Benefits Schedule reimbursement for comprehensive genomic profiling, and integration of digital-innovation platforms will be pivotal to achieving an internationally replicable model for responsible, population-wide precision oncology.

result.abstractText: Precision oncology has transformed cancer care globally through biomarker-driven and genomically guided treatment strategies. In Asia, where nearly 60% of the world's population resides, the implementation of molecular profiling presents both significant opportunities and unique challenges. Despite increasing adoption, precision diagnostics remain largely concentrated in urban and academic centers, with disparities in access, infrastructure, and expertise across the region. Advances in next-generation sequencing (NGS), including targeted gene panels, comprehensive genomic profiling, whole exome sequencing, and whole-genome sequencing, have enabled the identification of actionable alterations across multiple tumor types. Liquid biopsy approaches, including circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs), are further transforming cancer care by enabling real-time disease monitoring and detection of resistance mechanisms. Integration of multiomics platforms is increasingly enhancing clinical decision-making. Molecular tumor boards play a critical role in interpreting complex genomic data and facilitating genomically guided treatment decisions, including targeted therapy selection, off-label treatment recommendations, and clinical trial enrollment. However, several barriers continue to limit widespread implementation of genetic testing in Asia, including high costs, limited reimbursement, inadequate infrastructure, lack of trained personnel, and insufficient genomic databases representing Asian populations. This review provides a comprehensive overview of current molecular diagnostic approaches, clinical applications, and evolving precision oncology practices in Asia. We also highlight key challenges and propose practical solutions, including physician and patient education, expansion of trial-matching platforms, and development of region-specific genomic datasets. Strengthening these areas will be essential for advancing equitable, accessible, and effective precision cancer care across Asia.

result.abstractText: The fragmentation of sensitive medical data across institutions and stringent privacy regulations creates isolated data silos, hindering the development of robust AI-driven healthcare solutions. Existing approaches often lack sufficient trust mechanisms, comprehensive auditability, and dynamic access control for multi-center collaboration. Goal: This protocol aims to resolve the tension between collaborative utility and data sovereignty by integrating federated learning (FL) with blockchain technology, providing a secure, auditable, and scalable framework for medical data sharing. The framework employs a tripartite architecture: cryptographic FL with adaptive regularization and Paillier homomorphic encryption for privacy-preserving local training; a multi-channel, tiered-sharding blockchain for decoupled access control, data provenance, and FL operation logging; and a dynamic privacy-computation coordination mechanism that adapts differential privacy and cryptographic protocols based on data sensitivity and hardware capability. The workflow follows a sequential set of steps, including data preprocessing, local encrypted gradient generation, blockchain-backed secure aggregation, and global model updating. Under experimental conditions, the framework achieved 92.5% model accuracy after 20 training rounds and supported up to 30 nodes. No raw data exposure was detected, and tamper detection succeeded in all evaluated test cases. The architecture reduced computational overhead by 41% compared to a centralized baseline, achieved 96% automated regulatory compliance for audited access approvals, and demonstrated linear scalability, with the block generation interval stabilizing at 4.2 s.

result.abstractText:
Background

Gallbladder carcinoma (GBC) is the most common biliary tract malignancy and is usually diagnosed at an advanced stage. Artificial intelligence (AI), including radiomics, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), is increasingly applied to its diagnosis, surgical management and prognostication, but how far the reported performance can be trusted is unclear.

Methods

PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library and Google Scholar were searched to 5 May 2026 using database-specific search strategies. Each primary prediction-model study was characterized separately by design, number of centers and validation type (internal, temporal or external).

Results

Of 31 primary AI studies in GBC, 29 were retrospective, 22 were single-center and 24 reported internal validation only. In independent test or external cohorts, DL and ML models discriminated benign from malignant gallbladder lesions with areas under the curve (AUCs) of approximately 0.80-0.89; a multicenter model distinguishing xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis from GBC achieved an external AUC of 0.88, and automated computed tomography (CT) segmentation an external Dice score of 0.76. The best recurrence model achieved an AUC of 0.76 on internal (random-split) validation; none of the reviewed prognostic models reported a quantified external-validation estimate. Intraoperative AI is technically feasible but has no outcome data, and federated learning has been tested only in simulation.

Conclusion

AI could plausibly assist several steps of GBC care, but the evidence is dominated by retrospective, single-center, internally validated studies from Asia, and metrics from different studies are not directly comparable. Prospective multicenter external validation, shared annotated datasets and standardized reporting are required before clinical adoption.

result.abstractText:
Background

Perineural invasion (PNI) in tongue squamous cell carcinoma (TSCC) is associated with aggressive behavior and poor outcomes, yet it can be under-recognized on H&E sections because it is often focal and interpretation varies. Manual assessment of PNI suffers from significant interobserver variability, motivating AI-based decision support. We developed and externally validated a weakly supervised WSI model to predict PNI in TSCC.

Methods

We retrospectively analyzed 1,511 digitized H&E whole-slide images from 629 patients at two centers. Patient-level partitioning yielded an internal training cohort of 305 patients and 787 WSIs, an internal validation cohort of 132 patients and 340 WSIs, and an external test cohort of 192 patients and 384 WSIs. Non-overlapping tiling generated 41,552,500 candidate patches before tissue-background exclusion, of which 7,813,555 unique tissue patches were retained for analysis. A two-stage pipeline was used: patch-level modeling and MIL-based slide aggregation. ResNet50 was selected over Inception_v3 and SimpleViT as the feature extractor. Patch-level prediction probabilities and image features were aggregated into a 101-dimensional patch likelihood histogram (PLH) and a 101-dimensional visual bag-of-words (BoW) representation, respectively. For conventional classifiers, the two representations were concatenated into a 202-dimensional vector, followed by z-score normalization and LASSO feature selection. For the Transformer, the two representations were processed separately using PCA, independently projected into 128-dimensional embedding spaces, and integrated using four-head cross-attention. Performance was assessed by ROC, decision curve analysis (DCA), and calibration.

Results

The internal training, internal validation, and external test cohorts included 305, 132, and 192 patients, respectively. PNI prevalence was 82.3%, 79.5%, and 72.9% in these cohorts, respectively. The Transformer fusion model achieved AUCs of 0.990 in the training cohort, 0.968 in the internal validation cohort, and 0.940 in the external test cohort. Calibration and decision curve analysis were used to characterize the model's predicted probabilities and modeled net benefit in the retrospective study cohorts. Patch-level Grad-CAM was used to generate qualitative saliency visualisations associated with ResNet50 patch-level PNI scores.

Conclusions

This externally validated computational pathology application demonstrated retrospective technical feasibility for WSI-level PNI prediction in TSCC and has potential clinical utility for flagging slides for focused pathologist review. Its effects on clinical workflow and postoperative decision-making require prospective evaluation.

result.abstractText: Recurrence in oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma (TSCC) remains a prognostic challenge, which necessitates additional prognostic approaches reflecting tumor biology. Therefore, we developed an objective, observer-independent, multiparametric model incorporating features of the tumoral and stromal compartments. Digitized whole-slide images from 80 patients with TSCC were analyzed using a combination of semi-automatic and deep learning-based approaches. We extracted quantitative histomorphological features, including tumor/stroma ratio (TSR), lymphocyte/stromal cell ratio in the tumor stroma (LSCR), and the modified Polsby-Popper (MPP) score reflecting tumor disjointedness. Human trophoblast cell surface glycoprotein (Trop-2) expression was assessed by immunohistochemistry in central and invasive-front tumor regions sampled via tissue microarrays (TMA) and quantified using the H-score. A composite score (CS) was constructed by summing points from these parameters; as Trop-2 did not improve cross-validated discrimination, a final three-marker CS (TSR, LSCR, MPP) was adopted as the final model. Patients were stratified into prognostic groups and recurrence-free survival (RFS) was analyzed. While individual parameters showed only trends, the CS stratified patients into poor, intermediate and favorable prognosis groups with 5-year RFS probabilities of 64.6%, 75.3%, and 100.0%. Repeated five-fold cross-validation yielded a cross-fitted consensus concordance index of 0.587 (mean per-repetition concordance index 0.567 ± 0.039), compared with an apparent concordance index of 0.676, with no evidence of a difference from conventional prognostic factors. In exploratory multivariable Firth-penalized Cox regression adjusted for pT3-pT4a category, the favorable group showed a lower recurrence hazard than the poor group (HR 0.104, 95% CI 0.001-0.854, p = 0.0316); this non-cross-validated estimate is fragile given the small favorable group without recurrence events. This observer-independent whole-slide image approach may provide complementary prognostic information to conventional histological features but requires external validation.

result.abstractText: The immune-fibrotic axis functions as a vicious feedback loop where age-related chronic, low-grade systemic inflammation (inflammaging) drives maladaptive tissue repair and fibrosis, while senescent fibrotic cells in turn amplify systemic inflammation. In the aging heart, immune dysregulation and fibroblast activation drive tissue scarring and stiffening and a higher risk of heart failure and vascular disease. To identify cardiac regions and cell types affected with age, we monitored transcriptional changes across whole hearts of 6- and 24-month-old male and female mice. Spatially resolved signatures of macrophages and fibroblasts, non-cardiomyocyte populations highly involved in inflammaging, were enriched predominantly in the valves and aorta. With age, two cell types simultaneously adopted maladaptive programs: Macrophages displayed reduced immune homeostasis together with increased chemotactic and stromal programs, while more widely distributed fibroblast-lineage cells displayed alterations in extracellular matrix organization and intercellular signals, as well as upregulation of senescence-associated Cdkn1a (encoding p21) and other activated features shared with human cardiac fibroblasts. The major biological significance of these findings is that cardiac immune-fibrotic remodeling is not a uniform, heart-wide process. Instead, it varies with cell type, with valves and aorta emerging as major sites where age-associated programs converge to progressively compromise cardiac structure and function.

Purpose

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to neuroimaging, electrophysiology, clinical text, and digitally measured behavior, but reported performance often exceeds the maturity of clinical evidence.

Method

We conducted a structured narrative review, informed by SANRA principles, of English-language human studies, reviews, and regulatory sources identified in PubMed/MEDLINE and IEEE Xplore from January 2022 through July 2026; older landmark studies were retained when necessary for historical or methodological context. We applied a common translational-evidence framework across six prespecified neurological domains to distinguish technical performance from external validation, prospective clinical evaluation, implementation, and demonstrated patient benefit. Evidence was appraised according to cohort representativeness, patient-level data separation, external and prospective validation, calibration, clinical comparators, regulatory status, workflow integration, and patient-level benefit.

Finding

Across stroke, dementia, Parkinson disease, epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, and neuro-oncology, the strongest evidence concerns narrowly defined imaging and signal-processing tasks. A cluster-randomized stroke study demonstrated shorter thrombectomy workflow time, and several externally validated models show improved portability. Long-term data for digital therapeutics in urinary incontinence are scarce. We assessed whether improvements with app-based multimodal therapy are sustained over 48 weeks, and outcomes after a 12-week delay in initiation.

result.abstractText: Rapid tests will likely become increasingly available to crime scene investigators and have the potential to fundamentally change how decisions are made during the examination of the crime scene. By speeding up the analysis of traces, preliminary results from on-site rapid testing can already be used to support decision-making at the crime scene and may ultimately transform how crime scenes are examined. However, crime scene investigators' decision-making remains influenced by cognitive factors that also affect current examination practices. Given the lack of practical guidance on decision-making in guidelines and forensic science handbooks, it is essential to understand how crime scene investigators make decisions in practice. In this scoping literature review (N = 32), we examine how crime scene investigators search for, interpret, collect, and analyse traces, and how the introduction of rapid tests may influence these decision-making processes. The review reveals that guidelines and handbooks have paid little attention to cognitive factors that may shape investigators' observations and decisions. Empirical studies, however, show that cognitive factors play an important role in the decision-making at the crime scene. Understanding these influences is becoming increasingly important as rapid testing may affect early decision-making and, in turn, may iteratively shape the course of the investigation. Further research is therefore needed to better understand how rapid testing may influence decision-making at the crime scene.

Purpose

To report a case of medulloepithelioma treated with palladium-103 (103Pd) plaque brachytherapy, followed by adjunctive continuous periodic intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy, highlighting a novel combined strategy for tumor control and management of its neovascular complications.

103Pd plaque brachytherapy was used to control a ciliary body medulloepithelioma. result.abstractText: Multimodal imaging is central to the diagnosis, staging, and management of bone tumors. Radiography and computed tomography remain essential for initial assessment and cortical evaluation, magnetic resonance imaging provides superior soft tissue contrast and local staging accuracy, and positron emission tomography enhances detection of metastatic disease and treatment response. No single technique suffices across clinical scenarios. Advances in artificial intelligence and radiomics offer avenues to augment this framework, with demonstrated potential in lesion classification, segmentation, prognostication, and response prediction. This review advances a specific argument rather than surveying available technologies: that the principal constraint on artificial intelligence in musculoskeletal oncology is the stability of the reference standard rather than algorithmic capability. Ground truth in bone tumors is unstable on four grounds. Core needle biopsy samples a limited volume and may miss the highest-grade component: agreement between biopsy and resection grade in central chondrosarcoma falls from a weighted kappa of 0.63 in long bones to 0.12 in the pelvis. Expert interpretation is itself inconsistent, with interobserver kappa for grading cartilaginous tumors of 0.44 among musculoskeletal pathologists and 0.35 among radiologists. Molecular criteria have redefined entities within the past decade, so older datasets contain classes that no longer exist as defined. And histological classification does not reliably predict clinical behavior. Consequently, measurable accuracy has a ceiling set by the reference standard rather than the algorithm, and apparent failure on external validation may reflect label divergence between institutions rather than model deficiency. Evidence is graded throughout, and clinical readiness distinguished from technical performance. No system for primary bone tumor characterization has regulatory clearance in the United States or Europe, and formal appraisal of this literature confirms low methodological compliance and infrequent external validation. Progress will depend on multicenter validation and protocol harmonization, and, distinctively for this field, on composite reference standards, outcome-based endpoints, and explicit uncertainty modelling, since ground-truth instability can be mitigated but not eliminated.

Background

Gastrointestinal (GI) diseases such as colorectal cancer and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) contribute substantially to global morbidity, with colorectal cancer accounting for nearly 10% of all cancer diagnoses worldwide. Many existing artificial intelligence (AI) models suffer from limited generalizability and poor clinical interpretability. This study aimed to develop and evaluate an explainable AI (XAI) framework for classifying GI diseases from endoscopic images.

Methods

Public datasets from the Simula Research Laboratory were used: Hyper-Kvasir (10,662 images) for training, Kvasir-V1 (4,000 images) for validation, and Kvasir-V2 (8,000 images) as an independent test set. Two convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, GastroNet-dilated multi-scale attention (DMSA) (a proposed DMSA Network) and M2ShallowNet (a lightweight hybrid model), were designed for complementary feature extraction. Deep features were fused using a dual context attentive feature network (DCAF-Net) followed by Aquila Optimizer (AO)-based feature-weight refinement without introducing additional trainable fusion parameters. Performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, and statistical testing. Interpretability was examined using gradient-weighted class activation mapping++ (Grad-CAM++) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP).

Results

The best-performing classifier, a multilayer perceptron (MLP), achieved an accuracy of 97.21%, precision of 97.27%, recall of 97.21%, Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 96.82%, and F1-score of 97.21% on the independent test set. ROC analysis demonstrated excellent class separability, and statistical testing confirmed reliable generalization. XAI results highlighted regions that qualitatively correspond to pathological areas; formal clinical validation of these interpretations was not performed in this study.

Conclusions

The proposed framework offers a promising research prototype for AI-assisted GI disease classification. Its potential for real-world endoscopic deployment requires further prospective validation before clinical adoption.

Background

Cerebral tuberculomas and brain metastases of bronchial carcinoma are often indistinguishable on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), leading to misdiagnosis. This study develops a contrast-enhanced MRI radiomics-based nomogram to accurately differentiate them.

Methods

A total of 482 patients (290 males, 192 females; mean age 56.08±12.96 years), including 254 with cerebral tuberculomas and 228 with brain metastases of bronchial carcinoma were enrolled from two centers. Radiomic features were extracted, standardized, and reduced via significance testing, Pearson correlation, and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. A radiomic model was built, then integrated with clinical predictors into a nomogram. Performance was assessed across training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, calibration, and decision curve analysis (DCA).

Results

A total of 13 radiomic features were selected for model development. The radiomic model demonstrated areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.907, 0.891 and 0.886 in training, internal validation, and independent external validation cohorts, respectively, significantly outperforming models based solely on clinical factors, which achieved AUCs of 0.781, 0.712, and 0.828 (P<0.05). The nomogram, which integrated the radiomic scores (Rad-scores), age, ring enhancement, meningeal thickening, and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels, exhibited superior performance with AUCs of 0.951, 0.937, and 0.940 across the three cohorts. DCA demonstrated that the nomogram provided greater clinical net benefits across a range of threshold probabilities, and calibration curves indicated strong consistency between predicted probabilities and actual outcomes.

Conclusions

A nomogram combining clinical factors and contrast-enhanced MRI radiomics accurately differentiates cerebral tuberculomas from brain metastases of bronchial carcinoma, offering robust decision support for individualized diagnosis and treatment.

result.abstractText: Colorectal liver metastases (CLM) exhibit distinct histopathological growth patterns (HGPs) at the metastasis-liver interface, clinically relevant for prognosis and potential predictive value. This study investigates the feasibility of using Fluorine-18 Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography Computed Tomography (<sup>18</sup>F-FDG PET/CT) to preoperatively classify HGPs in CLM and secondly investigate PET parameters as prognostic markers for overall survival (OS). In a prospective study at Umeå University Hospital (June 2013-December 2017), 78 patients with resectable CLM underwent contrast-enhanced liver MRI and <sup>18</sup>F-FDG PET/CT imaging. HGP classification was performed on tissue sections according to 2017 international guidelines. PET features (SUV<sub>mean</sub> [standardised uptake value], SUV<sub>max</sub>, metabolic tumour volume [MTV] and first-order texture metrics) were analysed to distinguish encapsulating (eHGP) from replacement (rHGP) patterns. In pretreated patients, multivariate logistic regression including both metabolic and texture parameters identified significant associations for parameters from the fixed level threshold algorithm (VuePoint Sharp IR) with small odds ratios. Overall, PET parameters showed limited ability to discriminate between eHGP and rHGP. OS was superior with eHGP versus rHGP (log-rank p = 0.045). In chemonaïve patients, SUV-based metrics showed unadjusted exploratory associations with OS after liver surgery, varying by reconstruction/delineation and were not significant after correction for multiple testing. FDG-PET-derived parameters were not reliably associated with HGP and did not support non-invasive HGP prediction in this cohort. eHGP was associated with superior survival, underscoring the value of HGP assessment for prognostication while alternative non-invasive biomarkers remain to be identified.

Objectives

Brain metastasis (BM) frequently occurs in advanced cancer patients, and accurate identification of the primary origin is essential for personalized treatment. Conventional imaging often lacks sensitivity and specificity for BM source prediction. This study aimed to develop and validate a multiparametric MRI-based radiomics model emphasizing brain-tumor interface (BTI) features to improve noninvasive BM origin identification.

Materials and methods

The primary cohort included 429 patients (740 BMs) from two centers, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), small cell lung cancer (SCLC), breast cancer (BC), and gastrointestinal cancer (GIC), and an independent validation cohort of 33 patients (84 BMs) from a third center. All underwent pre-treatment 3.0 T MRI with T1-weighted contrast-enhanced (T1CE) and T2-weighted (T2W) sequences. Radiomic features were extracted from tumor core and BTI regions (2, 4, 6, 8 mm). Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used for feature selection, and radiomics signatures (RS) were evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis.

Results

The constructed RS-BTI4 based on the 4-mm BTI region generated the best overall performance, with area under the ROC curve (AUCs) in the training cohort were 0.855 (LC/NLC), 0.910 (SCLC/NSCLC), and 0.890 (BC/GIC); in validation cohort, 0.726, 0.856, and 0.809; and in external validation cohort, 0.739, 0.750, and 0.792, respectively. RS-BTI4 consistently outperformed models based on other BTI radial widths and the whole tumor region in identifying the primary origin of BM.

Conclusion

BTI-derived radiomic features demonstrate strong potential for noninvasive identification of BM origin, with the 4-mm BTI region showing optimal predictive performance.

Key points

Question Conventional MRI cannot reliably identify the primary origin of brain metastases, particularly when the primary tumor remains unknown at diagnosis. Findings The 4-mm brain-tumor interface model showed the most favorable overall performance, measured by area under the curve, across three binary classification tasks and validation cohorts. Critical relevance statement Integrating brain-tumor interface radiomics with multiparametric MRI may improve noninvasive estimation of BM origin and support more targeted diagnostic evaluation in clinical radiology.

Background

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the most common malignant tumors in China, and its prognosis is affected by many factors, such as tumor stage, liver function status, and patient health. To formulate treatment plans and evaluate prognosis, clinicians require accurate prediction of early postoperative recurrence of HCC. To address this clinical need, this study proposes a novel deep learning framework, termed MIFF-CLIP-HCC, to predict the early postoperative recurrence of HCC based on multimodal information fusion framework (MIFF) and Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP).

Methods

The MIFF-CLIP-HCC framework comprises two core steps. It first uses a fusion framework with a bidirectional attention mechanism to integrate multimodal information, including arterial phase images, venous phase images, and clinical data from patients with HCC. It then introduces image features extracted by the foundational CLIP model to deeply mine effective information from arterial and venous phase images, which increases the performance of the model.

Results

Between 2022 and 2025, a total of 240 early-stage HCC patients from two centers were included. Of these, 180 were from The First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University (Center 1) (including 114 early recurrence cases and 66 non-early recurrence cases, with an 8:2 ratio for training and internal testing), and the remaining 60 were from Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center (Center 2) (including 35 early recurrence cases and 25 non-early recurrence cases), designated as the external test cohort. The accuracy and robustness of the model were validated on internal and external test sets. The model achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.844 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.726-0.963] on the internal test set and 0.759 (95% CI: 0.651-0.867) on the external test set, outperforming other fusion frameworks (best baseline AUC: 0.779 on internal and 0.690 on external).

Conclusions

The results demonstrate that the proposed MIFF-CLIP-HCC framework, which employs dual optimization strategies of multimodal information fusion and CLIP, significantly improves the accuracy of early postoperative recurrence prediction for HCC, thus demonstrating considerable potential for clinical application.

Background and objective

Fatty infiltration of skeletal muscle and myocardium is associated with muscle dysfunction, myocardial fibrosis, and arrhythmias. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based fat quantification techniques are being increasingly applied in the skeletal muscle and myocardium, but no review has systematically compared measurements in these areas. The purpose of this review was to compare the quantification of skeletal muscle and myocardial fat in terms of technical principles, clinical applications, and research paradigms.

Methods

PubMed, Web of Science, relevant journal databases, and conference proceedings (e.g., Proceedings of the International Society for Magnetic Resonance in Medicine) were searched up to December 2025 for English-language literature with the following keywords: "MRI", "fat quantification", "Dixon", "magnetic resonance spectroscopy", "T1 mapping", "T2 mapping", "skeletal muscle", "myocardium", "epicardial adipose tissue", and "artificial intelligence". Original research, reviews, and consensus statements were included.

Key content and findings

Literature onthe Dixon method, magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), mapping techniques, magnetic resonance fingerprinting (MRF), and artificial intelligence (AI) was summarized. In skeletal muscle, the Dixon method is the practical standard, demonstrating robust multicenter reproducibility and established functional correlations in muscular dystrophy, sarcopenia, and inflammatory myopathies. In the myocardium, fat quantification relies mainly on mapping techniques, especially T1 mapping and epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) quantification, as Dixon and MRS techniques are limited by cardiac motion, thin walls, and low-fat content. Myocardial mapping detects subclinical injury, and increased EAT volume is independently associated with myocardial fibrosis. These techniques aid diagnosis and risk stratification in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, diabetic cardiomyopathy, and Fabry disease. AI is driving automated segmentation and prognostic prediction in both fields.

Conclusions

Skeletal muscle fat quantification is predominantly conducted with the Dixon method and is relatively mature, whereas myocardial fat quantification relies mainly on mapping techniques and lacks standardization. The multicenter validation of approaches related to skeletal muscle and related experiences in automated segmentation and AI application can inform practices in the quantification of myocardial fat. Combined cardiac-skeletal muscle assessment and integrated multiparametric imaging are promising future directions in the broader field.

result.abstractText: Evidence on the real-world impact of artificial intelligence (AI) decision support on diagnostic efficiency and workflow outcomes in primary breast cancer pathology remains limited. This retrospective, single-site, paired reader, two-arm study evaluated the impact of AI-assisted digital pathology (DP + AI) versus standard DP on workflow efficiency and diagnostic performance in digitized consecutive breast biopsy cases. Primary endpoints were pathologist review time, lab turnaround time (TAT), and usability (survey-based). Secondary endpoints included diagnostic performance of pathologists across both arms and standalone AI against adjudicated reference standard. Analyses included descriptive statistics, paired t-test, and diagnostic performance metrics with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The study included 194 digitized breast biopsies. The mean pathologist overall review time was reduced by 43.5% in DP + AI (40.18 [95% CI: 36.20-44.16] s) versus DP (71.12 [95% CI: 64.39-77.84] s) (p < 0.0001). Diagnostic agreement was 97.42% with DP and 99.48% with DP + AI, with 100% sensitivity observed in the DP + AI workflow. The standalone AI showed high diagnostic accuracy, with area under the curve values ≥0.99 across cancer subtypes. Usability survey showed high satisfaction, ease of use, and perceived clinical utility. Baseline TAT analysis of 3298 cases, independent of study cohort, showed longer TAT for cases requiring immunohistochemistry (IHC; 3.73 days) than for those not requiring (1.17 days). Retrospective workflow modelling suggested that AI-guided IHC pre-ordering could potentially reduce TAT by approximately 2.5 days for patients. DP + AI showed improvements in workflow efficiency while maintaining diagnostic performance. These findings suggest that integration of AI into routine breast pathology workflows may support faster diagnosis, optimized laboratory operations, and improved scalability.

Aims

Muscle biopsy assessment relies on descriptive features that are difficult to compare across samples. We developed MyoPath to quantify these features and examined their usefulness in clinical biopsies and population-based autopsy material.

Methods

MyoPath combines Cellpose-SAM and conventional image analysis within QuPath to segment myofibers, fat, nuclei, and connective tissue. We analyzed 478 hematoxylin and eosin images from HuashanMuscle (79 snap-frozen biopsies) and GTEx (399 formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded autopsy samples). Thirty-seven features were summarized by seven pathology indicators. A composite model trained on GTEx healthy and wasting strata was transferred to HuashanMuscle without retraining.

Results

Segmentation Dice coefficients ranged from 0.87 to 0.95 on annotated cryosections. Nuclear centralization index (NCI) and fiber size coefficient of variation (fiber CV) discriminated myopathy from controls in HuashanMuscle (AUC 0.85 and 0.79) and wasting from healthy donors in GTEx (0.74 and 0.74). Their GTEx associations changed little after age and sex adjustment. The composite achieved AUC 0.788 (95% CI 0.71-0.85) in GTEx and 0.873 (0.78-0.94) in HuashanMuscle. In the latter cohort, mean predicted probability was 0.49 compared with an observed myopathy proportion of 0.79.

Conclusions

NCI and fiber CV provide interpretable measures of muscle pathology in two distinct tissue settings. MyoPath supports quantitative comparison between groups; clinical severity grading and interpretation of absolute scores require further validation.

Background

Mitotic activity is a recognized marker of tumor proliferation, yet its reproducible assessment across whole-slide images (WSIs) remains difficult. We developed a transfer-learning framework for lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) and evaluated whether a patch-derived tumor-area mitosis proportion (TAMP) was associated with survival and molecular tumor characteristics.

Methods

The analysis combined MIDOG 2022 with TCGA-LUSC, including 478 patients and 512 diagnostic WSIs after quality control. Tumor regions and mitotic figures were reviewed by two pathologists with interobserver agreement of Cohen's κ ≥ 0.85. A ResNet-50 model was trained on MIDOG and subsequently adapted to TCGA-LUSC using Focal Loss and stain-aware augmentation. Target-domain performance was evaluated using patient-level stratified 5-fold cross-validation and an additional WSI-level holdout analysis to address potential leakage from the initial patch-level partitioning. TAMP was calculated from patient-level out-of-fold predictions as the proportion of evaluable tumor patches classified as mitosis-positive. Associations with overall survival, immune and genomic features, transcriptomic programs, predicted drug response, and transcription-factor activity were subsequently examined. Multivariable Cox regression adjusted for age, sex, smoking status, tumor stage, and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status.

Results

The model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.975 (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.965-0.980) on the held-out MIDOG test set. In TCGA-LUSC, fine-tuning increased the initial patch-level AUC from 0.82 to 0.92. Patient-level cross-validation yielded a mean AUC of 0.89 (95% CI: 0.86-0.90), and WSI-level holdout validation yielded an AUC of 0.90 (95% CI: 0.84-0.90). High TAMP was associated with poorer overall survival (log-rank p = 0.008; HR = 1.82, 95% CI: 1.18-2.81) and remained associated with mortality after multivariable adjustment (adjusted HR = 1.68, 95% CI: 1.08-2.62; p = 0.022). Higher TAMP was also associated with lower stromal fraction, selected immune-cell differences, greater indel-derived neoantigen load and indel burden, and enrichment of stem-cell proliferation, growth-factor-response, E2F-target, G2M-checkpoint, and MYC-target programs. Additional associations were observed with predicted sensitivity to selected cell-cycle-targeting compounds and with proliferation-related transcription-factor activity.

Conclusions

TAMP provides a patient-level, image-derived representation of mitosis-positive tumor regions that was associated with survival and several molecular features in TCGA-LUSC. Its association with overall survival persisted after adjustment for major clinical covariates. External multicenter validation, prespecified threshold evaluation, and prospective assessment are required before clinical use.

Background and objective

The predictive value of prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) for extraprostatic extension (EPE) in prostate cancer remains unclear.

Objective

We assessed whether adding PSMA PET/CT to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and clinical factors improves side-specific EPE prediction.

Methods

Patients undergoing PSMA PET/CT and MRI before radical prostatectomy were analysed retrospectively. The endpoint was side-specific EPE (≥pT3a). Predictors were selected by backward elimination, and the final nomogram was fitted using generalised estimating equations to account for clustering of lobes within patients. Discrimination, calibration, and net benefit were assessed, with external validation in an independent single-centre cohort.

Results and limitations

Development and validation cohorts included 801 and 287 lobes. The final model comprised prostate-specific antigen density (odds ratio [OR] 1.54 [95% confidence interval {CI} 0.94-2.50]; biopsy International Society of Urological Pathologists grade group (2 vs benign/1: OR 2.01 [95% CI 1.27-3.19]; 3 vs benign/1: OR 3.82 [95% CI 2.30-6.35]; 4 vs benign/1: OR 2.50 [95% CI 1.54-4.08]; 5 vs benign/1: OR 4.05 [95% CI 2.18-7.53]), MRI T-stage (organ-confined with a lesion [OC] vs organ-confined with no lesion [NL]: OR 1.31 [95% CI 0.86-1.99]; EPE vs NL: OR 4.11 [95% CI 2.56-6.60]), PSMA T-stage (OC vs NL: OR 1.67 [95% CI 1.07-2.61]; EPE vs NL: OR 2.59 [95% CI 1.49-4.49]), PSMAtotal (OR 1.72 [95% CI 1.33-2.23]). In development, the PSMA-MRI nomogram showed superior discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] 0.80 vs 0.71, p < 0.001). On validation, the updated model demonstrated discrimination comparable to the reference model (AUC 0.85 vs 0.86, p = 0.9), with minor risk overestimation and similar net clinical benefit. Limitations include a relatively small validation cohort.

Conclusions

The PSMA-MRI nomogram appeared to outperform the MRI-only model in development, but this was not confirmed in validation, indicating limited, context-dependent incremental value.

result.abstractText: Neoadjuvant therapy is an emerging strategy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), particularly in cases with technically resectable but biologically high-risk disease. Neoadjuvant therapy aims to reduce tumor burden and postoperative recurrence risk in high-risk HCC, while also providing a unique opportunity to preoperatively remodel the tumor microenvironment (TME). Recent advances in spatial multiomics have shown that the HCC immune microenvironment is highly heterogeneous, with distinct immune landscapes across the tumor core, invasive front, and adjacent liver tissue. At the spatial level, neoadjuvant therapy may reorganize the HCC tumor microenvironment beyond simple changes in immune-cell abundance. It reshapes the localization and interaction networks of tumor, immune, stromal, and vascular cells, including immune-cell infiltration into tumor nests, tumor-immune cell proximity, vascular accessibility, fibrotic exclusion barriers, and residual resistant niches. Collectively, these spatial changes influence pathological response, microvascular invasion, recurrence risk, and perioperative decision-making. However, key challenges include optimal patient selection, response evaluation, treatment sequencing, surgery timing, and perioperative safety management. Future integration of spatial omics, ctDNA, radiomics, digital pathology, and artificial intelligence may enable further developments in biology-guided neoadjuvant therapy and precise perioperative management of HCC.

result.abstractText: Neuroimaging research faces five linked barriers: technical complexity, prohibitive costs, lack of transparency, scattered infrastructure, and limited computational resources. Current platforms address these challenges one at a time. As a result, researchers must choose between convenience, transparency, and flexibility. We introduce NeuroStage, a unified, web-based platform that addresses all five barriers together. Technical complexity is removed through a simple interface that requires no programming skills. It supports automatic data upload, anonymisation, organisation of MRI data using the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) format, and standard preprocessing pipelines. Prohibitive costs are addressed through low-cost open access. The platform can be deployed in the cloud or locally, which also allows processing of protected health information with the same user experience. Lack of transparency is resolved through interactive viewers that let researchers check BIDS classification results and quality control reports before preprocessing begins. This prevents wasted computation on low-quality data. Scattered infrastructure is solved by providing a single platform that handles the entire workflow from scanner to ready-to-use processed and validated data for statistical testing. It also includes a collaborative data repository with secure transfer protocols and metadata-based data sharing. Limited computational resources are addressed by providing server infrastructure through the NeuroStage website. Researchers can run all processing directly from their browser without needing their own computing setup. This is further supported by checkpoint-based fault recovery, which saves completed stages. If processing fails, it can resume from the failure point rather than starting over. Using a multimodal imaging dataset, we show that NeuroStage can detect BIDS misclassifications, perform quality control, and reduce recovery time from preprocessing failures. NeuroStage successfully processed T1-weighted, T2-weighted, diffusion-weighted, resting-state functional, and pseudocontinuous Arterial Spin Labeling MRI using a publicly available toolbox for respective data acquisition without errors. Additionally, NeuroStage provides full quality control reports and detailed processing logs. A demo website showing most of the platform features is available at (https://neurostagedemo.onrender.com/, https://github.com/EN4D2-Computational-Lab/NeuroStage-EN4D2.git). This is currently a proof-of-concept, and continued work towards a public release is ongoing. NeuroStage aims to bring reliable and reproducible neuroimaging analysis to all researchers, including those without access to costly or advanced technology.

result.abstractText:
Background and objective

Since its pivotal introduction in 2011, gadoxetic acid has fundamentally revolutionized the landscape of hepatobiliary imaging in China, shifting the diagnostic paradigm from morphological assessment toward functional hepatocyte-level evaluation. This review comprehensively summarizes its 15-year clinical evolution within the Chinese healthcare system, exploring its pharmacological benefits, advanced applications, and future integration with data-driven frameworks.

Methods

A systematic literature search was conducted across major electronic databases, including PubMed, Web of Science, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure, spanning from 2011 to 2026. The search targeted peer-reviewed articles, consensus statements, clinical guidelines, and high-impact reviews published in English and Chinese regarding gadoxetic acid-enhanced liver magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

Key content and findings

Gadoxetic acid provides high sensitivity for early small hepatocellular carcinoma (sHCC) detection via specific OATP1B3 uptake. Beyond lesion detection, its quantitative mapping shows potential for estimating hepatic functional reserve (HFR) and risk stratification for post-hepatectomy liver failure. Crucially, the ongoing paradigm shift toward integrating radiomics and deep learning bridges macroscopic imaging and microscopic molecular biology, theoretically enabling a multi-dimensional profile of liver parenchyma and lesions within a single diagnostic session. However, a significant gap remains between retrospective predictive performance and clinical readiness, and these data-driven frameworks currently serve as supplementary investigational engines rather than standalone clinical decision-makers. Moving forward, integrating these high-dimensional signatures into constructs such as "digital twin" represents the next frontier. Furthermore, China's hepatitis B virus-dominant epidemiological cohorts, comprehensive multi-modal datasets, "Med-Engineering" fusion, and collaborative networks uniquely accelerate the development and preliminary validation of these models, offering valuable insights for global precision hepatology within China's healthcare system.

Conclusions

Over the past 15 years, gadoxetic acid has evolved far beyond a conventional liver imaging tool in China. While clinical translation of advanced analytics requires rigorous, prospective multicenter validation to ensure safety, combining this functional imaging agent with data-driven frameworks represents a promising frontier to eventually optimize future radiology workflows and support personalized precision hepatology.

Background

Accurate identification of residual axillary lymph node (ALN) disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) is essential for treatment planning and for evaluating potential surgical de-escalation. We assessed the diagnostic performance of conventional ultrasonography (US), shear-wave elastography (SWE), artificial intelligence (AI)/radiomics, and multimodal ultrasound-based models for post-NAC axillary restaging.

Methods

PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched from inception through December 2025. Histopathology after axillary surgery was the reference standard, and residual axillary nodal disease (ypN+) was uniformly defined as the positive target condition. Study-level 2×2 tables were harmonized to this direction. Risk of bias and applicability were assessed with the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS-2) tool. Bivariate random-effects models and hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) curves were used for modality groups with a sufficient number of independent studies; the positive likelihood ratio (PLR) and negative likelihood ratio (NLR) were pooled with random-effects models. Potentially overlapping cohorts were examined in sensitivity analyses. The study protocol was registered in PROSPERO (International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews; registration No. CRD420251271199).

Results

A total of 14 articles were included in the systematic review, 10 of which contributed 12 test-level datasets to the quantitative synthesis. For conventional US (six studies), the pooled sensitivity was 0.55 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.36-0.73], the pooled specificity was 0.79 (95% CI: 0.73-0.84), the area under the HSROC curve (AUC) was 0.78, and the pooled PLR and NLR were 2.47 (95% CI: 1.42-4.28) and 0.54 (95% CI: 0.30-0.95), respectively. AI/radiomics models (three studies) showed a pooled sensitivity of 0.93 (95% CI: 0.80-0.98), a specificity of 0.82 (95% CI: 0.60-0.94), and an AUC of 0.94; however, likelihood-ratio CIs were wide, and the bivariate covariance estimate reached the boundary. Evidence for SWE was limited to two potentially overlapping reports, and only one multimodal combined-model study had a complete harmonized 2×2 table. At a 40% pretest probability, a negative conventional US result reduced the posttest probability of residual nodal disease to approximately 26%.

Conclusions

Conventional US alone does not reliably exclude residual axillary nodal disease after NAC. AI/radiomics approaches show promising diagnostic performance, but the evidence for this is sparse, heterogeneous, and imprecise. The currently available data do not support definitive modality ranking or omission of axillary surgery on the basis of imaging alone, and prospective multicenter external validation is required.

Background

Microvascular invasion (MVI) is a critical risk factor for postoperative recurrence and metastasis in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC); however, reliable noninvasive preoperative prediction remains challenging. This study aimed to investigate the value of contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) in evaluating MVI in rabbit VX2 liver tumors.

Methods

Twenty healthy New Zealand rabbits were selected and used to establish VX2 liver tumor models. After 2 weeks, all models underwent conventional ultrasonography and CEUS with SonoVue (Bracco). We plotted time-intensity curves (TICs) to derive quantitative parameters, including mean intensity of the TIC (mTIC), peak intensity (PI), arrival time (AT), rise time (RT), time to peak (TTP), flow-out time (FT), and mean transit time (mTT). Based on histological diagnosis, tumors were classified into MVI and non-MVI groups. We compared the two groups in terms of the differences between VX2 tumors and the surrounding hepatic parenchyma.

Results

(I) Histological examination confirmed that 39 VX2 liver tumor models were successfully established in rabbits, with a tumor inoculation success rate of 97.50%. Among these, MVI was identified in 21 VX2 tumors. (II) Compared to tumors in the non-MVI group, those in the MVI group exhibited a larger diameter (P=0.01). Quantitative CEUS analysis revealed that the MVI group, compared to a non-MVI group, had a higher mTIC and PI (P=0.02 and P<0.001, respectively) and a shorter AT and TTP (both P values =0.03). (III) The RT of VX2 tumors was shorter than that of the surrounding liver parenchyma in both the MVI and non-MVI groups (P=0.002 and P=0.047, respectively). In the MVI group, the AT and TTP of the tumors were shorter (P=0.049 and P<0.001, respectively) while the PI was higher compared to the adjacent parenchyma (P=0.01). (IV) Receiver operating characteristic analysis showed that the PI achieved the highest diagnostic performance, with an area under the curve of 0.79 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.65-0.93].

Conclusions

Quantitative CEUS parameters provide crucial information for evaluating MVI in VX2 liver tumors. These findings constitute experimental evidence that supports the clinical assessment of tumor aggressiveness.

result.abstractText:
Background

The efficacy of immunotherapy among patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) varies, and thus reliable predictive biomarkers of response are needed. This study aimed to develop and validate a stacking ensemble learning model based on pretreatment positron emission tomography (PET) radiomics to predict response to immunotherapy in patients with NSCLC.

Methods

In this retrospective study, 45 patients with NSCLC treated with immunotherapy were enrolled. Pretreatment Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine-format PET images were preprocessed and normalized. Tumor volumes were segmented using three methods: manual delineation, fixed standardized uptake value (SUV) thresholding with a standardized uptake value of 2.5 (SUV2.5), and adaptive thresholding (40% of the maximum SUV). Radiomics features were extracted, followed by a multistep feature selection process involving mutual information, Spearman correlation, and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. Predictive models constructed included a stacking ensemble model [with k-nearest neighbors (KNN), logistic regression (LR), and random forest (RF) as base learners], a clinical feature-based model, and a deep learning model. Model performance was evaluated on an independent test set according to the area under the curve (AUC), accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score.

Results

On the test set, the stacking ensemble model achieved the highest predictive performance using features from the SUV2.5 segmentation dataset, with an AUC of 0.933 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.846-0.994]. This significantly outperformed the best single model (LR; AUC=0.896) and a deep learning model (AUC =0.925). The clinical feature-based model showed moderate predictive capability, with extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) yielding the highest AUC of 0.877 (95% CI: 0.644-1.000).

Conclusions

The proposed PET radiomics stacking ensemble model, which leverages features from multiple segmentation strategies, demonstrated superior predictive performance for immunotherapy response in NSCLC compared to single models and other benchmarks. This approach offers an effective strategy for enhancing robustness in small-sample radiomics studies and holds promise as a noninvasive decision-support tool that can aid in personalized immunotherapy stratification.

result.abstractText: Three-dimensional virtual histology using synchrotron radiation micro-computed tomography enables non-destructive visualization of biological tissue microarchitecture with isotropic resolution. Objective

To identify latent profiles of comprehensive needs among patients with gastrointestinal cancer receiving chemotherapy and examine factors associated with profile membership.

Methods

This cross-sectional study included 341 adults with gastrointestinal cancer receiving chemotherapy at a tertiary hospital in Qingdao, China, from October 2024 to June 2025. Participants completed the Comprehensive Needs Assessment Tool in Cancer (CNAT), Strategies Used by People to Promote Health, Family APGAR Index, Comprehensive Scores for Financial Toxicity based on Patient-Reported Outcome Measures, and Fear of Progression Questionnaire-Short Form. Latent profile analysis was conducted using the eight CNAT domain scores. Factors associated with profile membership were examined using multinomial logistic regression with the three-step approach.

Results

Three profiles were identified based on most likely class membership: low needs-information priority group (38.1%), moderate needs-balanced group (40.5%), and high needs-medical priority group (21.4%). Education level, primary tumor site, number of chemotherapy cycles, stage, financial toxicity, self-management efficacy, and fear of progression were associated with profile membership.

Conclusions

Comprehensive needs varied across three latent profiles. These exploratory profiles may support stratified needs assessment and supportive care planning. External validation in multicenter prospective studies is required before profile-based care is implemented.

Purpose

To characterize the distribution of central subfield thickness (CST) measured by spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) in a longitudinal cohort of Ebola virus-seronegative individuals in Liberia.

Design

Longitudinal cohort study.

Methods

Close contacts of Ebola virus disease (EVD) survivors enrolled in the PREVAIL III Eye Study in Monrovia, Liberia underwent comprehensive ophthalmic examinations and macular imaging with Cirrus 5000 SD-OCT over five annual study visits. Prior Ebola virus infection was assessed using anti-Ebola virus glycoprotein IgG serology, and seropositive close contacts were excluded. CST measurements and descriptive statistics were analyzed longitudinally. In a post hoc analysis, participants with uveitis or retinal pathology were excluded from analyses characterizing retinal thickness in otherwise healthy eyes. Statistical analyses were conducted using R.

Results

Among 644 seronegative close contacts who underwent baseline ophthalmic evaluation, 181 (28.1%) had complete CST measurements in at least one eye at baseline, increasing to 548 of 594 (92.3%) at the subsequent annual visit and 404 of 407 (99.3%) at the final study visit. Median CST for the overall cohort at baseline was 220.5 μm (interquartile range, 207-234 μm). After excluding participants with uveitis or retinal pathology, median baseline CST was 220 μm, with 5th and 95th percentiles of 190 and 254 μm, respectively. CST distributions remained relatively stable during four years of follow-up, with a median CST of 220 μm in the final year.

Conclusion

CST values in this seronegative cohort from Monrovia were toward the lower end of previously reported Cirrus-based reference distributions. In a subset free of inflammation or retinal pathology, CST showed similar distributions across study visits. These findings highlight the importance of generating local datasets to interpret OCT measurements.
